tagline: From log road to concrete mile, Woodward carries Detroit’s automobile history.
intro: Woodward Avenue runs north-northwest from Detroit toward Pontiac, through downtown, residential neighborhoods and commercial districts. North of McNichols Road it becomes a divided boulevard, with median crossovers for Michigan left turns. The Federal Highway Administration lists this 27-mile All-American Road for its automobile heritage, represented by industrial buildings, mansions, museums and cultural institutions.

The avenue followed the Saginaw Trail, which linked Detroit with Pontiac, Flint and Saginaw. Construction toward Pontiac began in 1817 with logs laid across the road and their gaps filled with clay or sand. The legislature authorized a private toll road in 1848; oak planks followed the next year. Concrete arrived between 6 and 7 Mile roads in 1909, and the full length was paved in 1916. Later widening required another change: Grand Trunk moved its tracks away from Woodward and built a new Detroit–Pontiac line between 1926 and 1930.

The corridor begins beside Hart Plaza, but its first block is a pedestrian plaza. Northbound, the avenue passes the Cultural Center, New Center and Highland Park before crossing into Ferndale. Continue through Pleasant Ridge, along Berkley’s edge, past Birmingham’s downtown bypass and through Bloomfield Hills to Pontiac. M-1 ends at Square Lake Road; Woodward itself continues to Pontiac’s downtown loop.

moments.title: Ford Piquette Avenue Plant
moments.text: East of Woodward, the Piquette Avenue Plant housed Ford’s early production in a building modeled after New England textile mills. Built in 1904, it has brick exterior walls pierced by 355 windows. The factory’s maple floors rest on square oak beams and posts. Here, workers experimented in 1908 by pulling a Model N chassis across the third floor on skids, adding its axles and wheels along the way. The first production Model T was completed here that September. Ford moved production to Highland Park in 1910; the formal moving assembly line followed there in 1913.
moments.notice: The brick factory’s 355 windows follow a design modeled after New England textile mills.

moments.title: 6 Mile to 7 Mile
moments.text: Between 6 and 7 Mile roads, Woodward received the country’s first mile of concrete roadway in 1909, at a cost of $14,000. Tolls on some stretches of the avenue had lasted as late as 1908. By 1916, its full length was paved. Changes in traffic control followed: a tower lifted a police officer above Woodward’s intersection with Michigan Avenue in 1917, then gave way to a four-way traffic light in 1920. McNichols Road occupies the 6 Mile position in Detroit’s numbered road system. At 6 Mile today, the avenue widens into a divided boulevard beside the Palmer Park area.
moments.notice: North of McNichols, the median and U-turn crossovers shape the boulevard.

moments.title: Woodward Dream Cruise
moments.text: The Dream Cruise follows Woodward from Ferndale to Pontiac on the third Saturday in August. Its beginnings were local: Ferndale mayor Pamela S. McCullough and plumber Nelson House proposed the event in 1994 to raise money for a children’s soccer field. Organizers expected 30,000 or 40,000 people at the first cruise in August 1995; about 250,000 came. Communities along the route collaborate on additional events, including Ferndale, Berkley, Birmingham and Pontiac. The event brings muscle cars, street rods, custom vehicles and collector cars along the corridor, with most displayed cars dating from the 1950s through the early 1970s.
